Inhibition means the act of holding something back, suppressing it, or preventing it from happening freely. Think of it as an internal brake — something that slows down, blocks, or restricts an action, feeling, process, or reaction.

The "something" being held back can be a feeling inside a person, a behavior, a biological process in the body, or even a chemical reaction in a lab. The word is used in very different fields, but the core idea stays the same: a force or factor that stops or limits something else.
1. In Everyday Life — Social and Emotional Inhibitions

This is the most common way you'll encounter the word.

When people talk about inhibitions in daily conversation, they usually mean the internal mental barriers that stop a person from acting freely, openly, or naturally — especially in social situations. These barriers usually come from fear, shyness, self-consciousness, embarrassment, or the worry of being judged by others.

Imagine someone who desperately wants to get up and dance at a wedding, but just... can't bring themselves to do it. They're afraid of looking silly. That fear is an inhibition — it's holding them back from doing something they'd otherwise enjoy.

Or think of someone who has a great idea in a meeting but stays quiet because they're too nervous to speak up in front of others. That nervousness is an inhibition too.

Inhibitions are not always bad. Some of them are actually healthy and necessary. For example:

  • The inhibition that stops you from shouting rude things at a stranger is a good one. It's your internal sense of decency holding back an impulse.
  • The inhibition that stops a child from running into a busy road is protective.

But many inhibitions are limiting. They prevent people from expressing themselves, enjoying life, forming connections, or achieving their potential — all because of irrational fear or excessive self-consciousness.

"Losing your inhibitions" is a very common phrase. It means letting go of those internal blocks and acting more freely and openly — doing what you feel without overthinking or fearing judgment. Alcohol, for example, is famously known to lower people's inhibitions, which is why people sometimes act more boldly or carelessly after drinking.

"Inhibited" as a description of a person means someone who is very restrained, guarded, self-conscious, or unable to express themselves naturally. An inhibited person holds a lot back.
2. In Psychology — The Mind Suppressing Itself

In psychology, inhibition has a more technical but related meaning. It refers to the mental process — conscious or unconscious — by which the mind suppresses an impulse, desire, thought, or emotion to prevent it from being expressed in behavior.

Your mind is constantly generating impulses — urges to react, to lash out, to say something, to do something. Inhibition is the psychological mechanism that filters those impulses and keeps many of them from actually becoming actions.

For example:

  • You feel a flash of anger at a friend. You want to say something harsh. But you hold it in and respond calmly instead. That holding-in process is inhibition.
  • A person has an urge to steal something from a shop. The thought of consequences — shame, guilt, getting caught — suppresses that urge. That suppression is inhibition.

The famous psychologist Sigmund Freud gave inhibition a very specific place in his theories. He saw inhibitions as the ego's way of controlling the raw, animalistic impulses of the unconscious mind — keeping them from breaking through into behavior inappropriately. In this framework, too much inhibition leads to psychological tension and inner conflict, because the suppressed impulses don't simply disappear; they get buried.
3. In Biology and Neuroscience — Suppressing Biological Processes

Here, inhibition refers to the reduction or blocking of a biological activity, function, or process in the body.

In the nervous system, neurons (brain cells) communicate with each other constantly. Some neurons, when they fire, excite neighboring neurons — encouraging them to activate. Other neurons do the opposite: they inhibit neighboring neurons, meaning they suppress their activity and prevent them from firing. This is called neural inhibition, and it is absolutely essential to how the brain works. Without inhibitory signals, your brain would be in a constant state of uncontrolled electrical activity (which is actually what happens during some types of epileptic seizures — when inhibitory mechanisms fail).

More broadly in biology:

  • A substance that slows down or stops a biological process (like the growth of a bacterium, the activity of a hormone, or the functioning of an enzyme) is called an inhibitor, and what it does is called inhibition.
  • Antibiotics, for example, work through inhibition — they inhibit the processes that allow bacteria to survive or reproduce.
  • Many medications work by inhibiting specific enzymes or receptors in the body to produce a desired therapeutic effect.

In chemistry, inhibition refers to the slowing down or stopping of a chemical reaction. A chemical inhibitor is a substance added to a reaction to reduce its rate or stop it entirely. This is used extensively in industry to prevent unwanted reactions — for example, adding inhibitors to materials to slow down corrosion (rusting) or to prevent food from spoiling too quickly.
The Thread That Connects Every Meaning

No matter where you see the word, the logic is always the same:

Something exists that could happen — a feeling, a behavior, a nerve firing, a chemical reaction — and inhibition is the force, mechanism, or state that holds it back, slows it down, or prevents it.

Think of inhibition as the opposite of expression, activation, or release.
Common Forms and Phrases to Know

• "Have no inhibitions" — to be completely free, open, and unafraid of judgment; to act without any internal restraint.
  • "Lower/lose one's inhibitions" — to become less guarded and more free in behavior, often temporarily.
  • "Free from inhibition" — acting naturally and openly, without fear or self-consciousness.
  • "Inhibition of [a process]" — the blocking or suppression of a specific biological, chemical, or psychological process.
  • An inhibition (countable) — a specific internal block or restraint a person carries. "She had many inhibitions around speaking in public."
  • Inhibition (uncountable) — the general state or quality of being inhibited, or the mechanism of suppression itself.

Understanding nearby words helps sharpen the meaning:

  • Restraint — very close in meaning; the holding back of impulses or feelings. Inhibition is slightly more internal and psychological; restraint can also refer to external control.
  • Suppression — actively pushing something down or keeping it from surfacing.
  • Self-consciousness — a cause of social inhibition; being overly aware of how you appear to others.
  • Repression — in psychology, a stronger, more unconscious version of suppression; burying something so deeply you're not even aware of it. Inhibition is generally more conscious.
  • Block — an informal synonym in some contexts ("a mental block").

The opposite of inhibition, in the social/emotional sense, is disinhibition — the state of acting without restraint, either because the normal inhibitory mechanisms have been removed (as by alcohol or certain drugs) or because the person naturally has very few barriers.

Inhibition is, in every sense, about something being held back or blocked from happening freely. In people, it most commonly means the emotional or psychological barriers — rooted in fear, shyness, or social norms — that prevent someone from acting naturally and openly. In science and medicine, it refers to the suppression or slowing of biological or chemical processes. The word always carries the idea of a restraining force working against free expression or activity.
